registry.searchable: Yes. registry.termsNote: No registry-specific terms of use were found; the page carries Crown copyright (King's Printer for Ontario). Ontario's copyright page allows non-commercial reproduction with credit and no changes, and says material 'may only be reproduced for commercial purposes under a licence.' The bulk BCIN dataset on the Ontario Data Catalogue is marked as not available for privacy reasons. Safest approach: deep-link the user to the registry search with suggested filters, show only what the user looks up, and don't scrape or store listings.

findings.why: The bedroom window looks small and high and may not meet the opening size.
findings.plain: Every floor level with a bedroom needs at least one outside window that opens from inside without tools, stays open by itself and gives an unobstructed opening of at least 0.35 m², unless that level has a door straight to the outside.
findings.title: Bedroom escape window: 0.35 m² opening

findings.why: The window opening looks small and may be under 380 mm.
findings.plain: The escape window's clear opening must be at least 380 mm in every direction; for sliders, measure only the part that opens.

findings.why: The inside view cannot show well size or cover.
findings.plain: If the escape window opens into a window well, keep at least 550 mm clear in front of it (beyond any outward-opening sash), and any well cover must open from inside without keys or tools.

fix.description: Install 5/8 in. Type X drywall on the suite ceiling and on both sides of dividing walls, keep it continuous and seal joints and penetrations; add self-closing doors where the separation has openings.

fix.costNote: Estimate, not a quote (Toronto, 2026, 'fire separation' line). Ceiling drywall installed and finished is $4.00-$6.50/sq ft before the Type X upgrade (see costs[]).

findings.why: Joists and ducts look exposed with no drywalled separation.
findings.plain: Separate the suite from the rest of the house with a 45-minute fire separation, or with a continuous smoke-tight barrier of 15.9 mm (5/8 in.) Type X drywall on both sides of dividing walls and under the floor/ceiling framing. The rating can be waived if the house is sprinklered.
findings.title: Fire/smoke separation between the two homes

source.title: 2024 Building Code Compendium (MMAH), Division B

fix.description: Enclose the furnace/water heater in its own room and line its walls (both sides) and ceiling with 5/8 in. Type X drywall.
fix.costNote: No separate price found; usually part of the fire separation work.

findings.why: Furnace and water heater look open to the basement with no separate room.

check.appliesWhen: a fuel-fired appliance serves both dwelling units

findings.plain: If the furnace or water heater serves both units, put it in a service room lined with 15.9 mm (5/8 in.) Type X drywall on both sides of its walls and on the underside of the ceiling framing; otherwise fuel-fired appliances need a 1-hour fire separation.
findings.title: Furnace room separation

source.title: 2024 Building Code Compendium (MMAH), Division B

fix.description: Install interconnected smoke alarms (hard-wired or wireless) with a visual (strobe) signal in both units and common areas.
fix.costNote: No standalone Ontario price found; one Toronto source bundles alarms into a $4,000-$8,000 electrical line (see costs[]).

findings.why: Smoke alarms in both homes, wired so they all sound together.
findings.plain: Put smoke alarms on every storey, in every bedroom and outside sleeping areas of each unit, and in shared exits and common areas, then interconnect them (hard-wired or wireless) so any one alarm sounds all alarms in both homes.
findings.title: Interconnected smoke alarms in both homes

source.title: 2024 Building Code Compendium (MMAH), Division B

fix.description: Add CO alarms beside each sleeping area in both units and in the furnace room, interconnected across the house.

findings.why: Carbon monoxide alarms near the bedrooms, linked together, when anything burns gas.
findings.plain: If the house has a fuel-burning appliance (such as a gas furnace or water heater) or an attached garage, put CO alarms next to the sleeping rooms in each unit and in the service room, interconnected so one alarm sounds all CO alarms in the house.
findings.title: Interconnected carbon monoxide alarms

source.title: 2024 Building Code Compendium (MMAH), Division B
source.section: 9.32.3.9C.(1) (interconnection within a house with a secondary suite)

findings.why: Stairs and a door are visible but the outside exit path is unclear.
findings.plain: Best: the suite has its own door to the outside. A shared exit is allowed if it is separated by a 30-minute fire separation, does not pass through the other home or a service room, and both homes have interconnected smoke alarms. Leaving through the other home is only allowed with an extra escape window and interconnected alarms, or if the house is sprinklered.
findings.title: A safe way out of the suite

source.title: 2024 Building Code Compendium, Division B Part 11

findings.question: Is there a door from the basement straight outside?

fix.description: Existing house: add a duct-type smoke detector interlocked to shut the furnace's fuel and power. Or give the suite its own heating (separate furnace or ductless heat pump) and seal the duct connections between units.

findings.why: Heating set up so smoke can't travel between the homes: a separate system or a smoke detector in the ducts.
findings.plain: Each home's air ducts may not be directly connected to the other home, and air from one suite may not be recirculated to the other. In a house 5+ years old, one existing forced-air system may serve both if each unit has smoke alarms and a duct smoke detector shuts off the furnace's fuel and power when it detects smoke.
